content.title: How would you rank Tiger Woods among the greatest golfers of all time?
content.text: How good a golfer was Tiger Woods?He was so good that, at one point in 2008, the gap between him at number 1 in the world and Phil Mickelson at number 2 was as big as the gap between Phil Mickelson and the golfer ranked at 1000. He was so good that, at the 2000 US Open, when no one else threatened to shoot under par for the tournament, he finished 12 under par, 15 shots better than his closest competitors. He was so good that, in his pomp, he won more than a third of the tournaments he entered in. Nowadays, if a player wins 5 or more tournaments in a year, it's a career-defining season. Really though, all these are consequences of what really separated him from everyone else: that he seemingly pulled off the shot he had to, without fail. It's as if the greater the pressure he was under, the more he would perform. Almost as though he would be bored by going through the motions and needed something extra to make it interesting for him. Perhaps most impressive, however, is that he still did the ordinary stuff better than anyone else.If Tiger Woods retired today, would he be considered the greatest golfer of all time?There's only three guys in the conversation: Bobby Jones, Jack Nicklaus and Tiger Woods. Hogan does not belong. It took Hogan quite a while to 'find' his swing. He was not a dominant player until well into his 30's. Every time Tiger, Jack and Jones played, they were favored. Everyone else was trying to beat them, not the course. And this was true from almost the start of their careers. In Jack and Tiger's case, from their junior/amateur careers. Think this is the hardest thing to do in sports, is win when everyone is expecting you to win. The extra layer of pressure is so hard, that it takes someone every special to perform under that kind of pressure. The only standards these three didn't exceed was probably their own very lofty ones. They expected to win every time, no matter how unrealistic that seems to the rest of us. So take your pick, but no else in golf history really belongs on that top rung. In my opinion.If Tiger Woods retired today, would he be considered the greatest golfer of all time?It's a great question and this debate will rage on for years to come. For me it's quite simple. Tiger Woods was unquestionably the greatest golfer of all time. I won't run through his achievements as this has already been eloquently outlined in previous answers. For me, Tiger Woods is a lot more than his winning record, or his dollars banked or his putting statistics in his prime - all of which, by the way, are nothing short of spectacular. Tiger was good in a way that the game had never witnessed before. Sure, Jack has won the most majors and by that measure, he will always be the greatest as I don't believe anyone will ever reach 18 majors again. But Tiger transcended the sport like nobody before him, and it's doubtful anybody ever will again. He transformed the game and its global appeal and there's no way the top 50 golfers in the world would earn the money they do now if it hadn't been for Tiger Woods. His foundation has raised millions of dollars for great causes, his career has inspired countless current pros (Jason Day and Rory McIlroy to name just two) and his impact on the sport has been immeasurable. On the course, Tiger was even more incredible. Nobody in the history of golf has shown such ability to destroy a field in the way he could. He was flawless, intimidating and at the time, incredibly long, and long-established pros would crumble when seeing him chasing through the field on a Sunday afternoon. He also had the most incredible resilience and determination - nothing seemed to faze him and he could just as easily follow a double-bogey with an eagle. Probably the most impressive thing about his game when he was at his best was his short range putting. From 10 feet and in, he was as close to perfect as anyone can be and when you hole almost everything in this range, you are going to win a lot of tournaments. It's a shame that he hasn't yet, and in my opinion won't ever, reach Jack's major record as that seems to be the only way the media measure his career. All his life he's been asked about Jack's record and it seems even he considers his own career somehow inferior to Jack's. But there's no doubt in my mind that he is the greatest golfer of all time.Toger Woods did everything in golf at an elite level. Few did anything as well as he did everything. At his peak, he won tournaments and majors at an unprecidented rate, some at incredible margins. He was dominant like no other male folfer had been. And then it fell apart. My theory has been that he didn't know how to age. That meant that instead of adapting to and working around its dininishing capabilities, he broke it trying to not have to. That's the thing about assessing his career. Judged by their best decade, no golfer comes close to him. He is the best of all time. Judged by the whole of their PGA careers, I think you have to give the nod to Nichlaus because… winning majors is how elite golfers are assessed. So, I’d put him as the 2nd greatest male golfer of all time. But, there is a very reasonable argument for putting him first.Managed VPS Hosting Made EasySkip setup and server stress. Explore VPS hosting plans.How good a golfer was Tiger Woods?I will shed a different perspective on Tiger since I played regularly with his father Earl at the Navy course in Cypress, Ca. I played golf with Tiger while he was about 9 yrs old through high school. Tiger was a plus 5 handicap at Navy by age 13. For those unfamiliar with handicapping, that’s giving the golf course back approximately 5 strokes! His stroke average at that age was around 67 for the championship, 7000 yard course. From my experience, this ability to score along with multiple US amateur championships makes Tiger the best junior golfer of all time. I was a first team all state high school golfer from Illinois in the early 70s with a 2 handicap. To put this into perspective against Tiger, he would have needed to spot me 7 strokes for 18 holes when he was still in junior high. I managed to beat him during a member guest tournament in the mid 90s when I shot 74 on a blustery day when Tiger hacked to a 75. He out drove me by 50 yards reaching par 5s with driver, and no more than 6 iron coming in. I made 7 birdies, 9 bogies and 2 pars that day while Tiger scored as bad as he ever had making no putts and 3 bogeys. I have competed against high level players and been on the periphery at one time. I have never seen the incredible power and control generated from a kid that was around 120 lbs at the time. Tiger truly played a game that was on an entirely different level than anyone since he was barely walking. Another incredible fact that is difficult to believe is when Tiger beat the pro at a local par three course in Long Beach when he was something like 5 years old! I spoke with the ...Is Tiger Woods now the greatest golfer ever, or is there more he has to do to take that title?Tiger Woods is the greatest golfer ever. People want to support Nicklaus here and the man was an incredible competitor in his day, but pure numbers do not support a case for Jack being better. We all know about the Majors 18 to 15 in favor of Jack. But let’s look at an objective measure of skill - what scores did they average over their career? Jack never won the Vardon Trophy awarded to the low scoring average for a PGA player over the course of a year. Now it may have been because he didn’t play the easiest courses on tour - the events like the GHO (Hartford) etc. where the winner could easily shoot -25 for the week. However Tiger generally didn’t either. So what is Tiger’s scoring average?He has led the PGA 9 times in overall scoringHe is the only man in history to average under 68 for a season. He did it twice.He basically averaged under 69 for 11 years in a row!Vardon Trophy - Wikipedia Now if you look at Jack’s averages it seems like he should have won it a couple years - but when compared to Tiger’s decade long dominance of this very objective category one can’t help but notice a stark difference. The Jack proponents argue that Nicklaus always finished in the Top Ten of every Major and was 2nd a lot etc. Which is true. But the depth of field in his day just wasn’t the same. Especially now that Tiger has shown he can beat a field consisting of Rory, DJ, Koepka, etc. etc. So while they are both great and stats can be manipulated to make a case for either man, the objective scores on paper make a very compelling case for Tiger being the greatest golfer ever.Ask a pro: "I'm 65 with $1M saved. What's my retirement budget?"This quiz matches nearly 50,000 people each month with vetted financial advisors.Is Tiger Woods now the greatest golfer ever, or is there more he has to do to take that title?I would make a distinction between Nicklaus and Woods as the greatest ever ‘golfer’. Nicklaus is the greatest golfer because the biggest test for any golfer will be Major championship course set ups. He has won the most so for me he is the greatest golfer. To compound that, consider that not only did he win 18 of them, he also finished 2nd outright or tied for 2nd 18 times in Major championships. Of the 40 majors played in the 1970's for example he finished in the top 10 in all but 4, missing only 1 cut. That is superb golf by any measure. He played consistently brilliant golf in a notoriously difficult game. Whether it was the slick greens at Augusta National or the tight fairways, the deep rough of a US Open or the inclement weather on the links courses for the Open Championship, Nicklaus was always there or thereabouts in the mix. For Woods, he never enjoyed the consistency in the Majors that Nicklaus had. He went through notable slumps during his peak years. He was still making cuts in the majors but he was finishing nowhere as he chose to go through a number of swing changes yet when his latest swing was fine-tuned and dialled in he was box office, absolutely electrifying and untouchable 15 times. Tiger Woods is the greatest professional golfer of all time. No question at all about it. A professional golfer is professional expressly to earn money. Tiger moved the needle big time, was a multi-millionaire before he even turned pro and is one of the wealthiest athletes in the world today. During Nicklaus’ prime he was part of what was deemed the ‘big three’ with Palmer and Player, both of whom assisted in growing the game worldwide. Tiger did that all by himself. He is the reason journeymen professionals on the PGA Tour get to play weekly for million dollar cheques, he is the reason the elite professionals (i.e. the guys who pick up a major or two, or who win big tournaments) are all multi-millionaires themselves. He helped make Golf a legitimate career for talented young amateurs as the financial rewards would be inevitable if they were successful. It was a calculated risk to turn professional during the Nicklaus era when a decent season would earn a golfer the equivalent of what a used car salesman made annually. You not only had to be good back then but you had to be very good to merely break even. Bearing that in mind, to suggest Nicklaus played against inferior opponents in his prime is disingenuous. Gary Player during a Skins match in 1983 won $170,000 during the event and was seen to be visibly shaking on the last hole. It was more money than he'd ever won in a year on the tour in his career, the man, a 9 time major winner, a legend in the game and he was incredulous that he'd won so much money and said he was in a state of shock and awe. Today a top pro can make that much money from having a logo on their cap or going to a few corporate shindigs every other month. That's not to mention the endorsement contracts and the huge increases in prize money since Woods' big bang moment at the 97 Masters. Tiger Woods is to be thanked for that. Nicklaus doesn't even come close in that regard. In summation - greatest golfer (skill, consistency, longevity) is Nicklaus, greatest Pro golfer (earnings, influence, profile) is Woods.Who is the greatest golfer ever, Jack Nicklaus or Tiger Woods?FYI - My answer was moved and I can’t get it back to the original question which was - Originally Answered: Who is the greatest golfer ever, Jack Nicklaus or Tiger Woods? So that’s why it doesn’t really make sense here on this question. Sorry… Both are undeniably great, and they are the clear 1–2 in the sport. So how do we determine which is the greatest, since there was no intersection of their careers? Here’s my take. I feel that Tiger in his prime was the most physically gifted player of all time. He dominated the sport like none before, and like none will likely ever do again. He intimidated every other player in the PGA with his length off the tee, his strength out of the rough, and his clutch putting. And yet, he only won 14 majors and in every single one he was leading going into the final round. You might also say that he had the greatest impact on the sport since Palmer, as today, virtually every top PGA player has emulated Tiger by using strength training to ensure that their bodies are in peak physical condition. Not to mention the impact Tiger has had on propelling the sport itself into the forefront of all major sports. But the question was “Who was the greatest GOLFER?” So not only did Jack win 18 majors, 4 more than Tiger has currently, he also finished second in 19 additional majors. Tiger has far less major runners up. Major Top 5s? Jack leads 55–31. Major Top 10s? Jack leads 66–38. Cha-Ching! Tiger at his best dominated everyone else in the field, but was often not at his best, even during his prime. He was on or off, while Jack was FAR more consistently great. And then there is the competition. Jack competed against many other Hall of Fame players such as Palmer, Trevino, Watson, Player, Snead, and numerous others during his career. All of these players won multiple majors competing against Jack. Tiger’s primary HoF competition during the prime of his career? Pretty much just Phil, and the tail end of Watson’s career. Are today’s golfers more physically talented across the board than in Jack’s time? Sure. But that’s irrelevant. Pluck Jack out of the 1950s & 1960s and plug him into the year 2000 and he too would be more fit and would have the advantage of today’s modern golf equipment. In other words, Jack, placed into Tiger’s era, might have been even better than Jack in his own era… Think on that for a minute. Jack Nicklaus IS the Greatest golfer of all time…Was Tiger Woods the greatest golfer of all time?“Was”, of course, implies past tense - and, of course, Tiger Woods is still competitive, so we don’t yet know the full extent of his career. So it’s hard to answer this question, because it requires knowing how “greatest” is defined … number of majors won, total number of victories, number of consecutive cuts made, best shot maker … there can be a lot of different criteria. I never thought Sam Snead’s 82 victories would ever be challenged. Tiger has 82. But I’ve never been fond of “Greatest of All Time” comparisons anyway, just because it requires comparing players from different eras under different levels of competition and different circumstances. But just to keep the discussion alive, here are a couple of stats about Tiger Woods that are mind boggling: He won three consecutive U.S. Junior Championships followed by three consecutive U. S. Amateur Championships before turning pro. He turned pro near the very end of a season - and won two of the remaining eight tournaments. He won his first PGA Tour tournament at age 20; his 25th at age 25; his 50th at age 30; and his 74th at age 36 - which included 14 majors and 18 World Golf Championships and a period of seven years without missing a cut. Any of those five year intervals would have made him eligible for the World Golf Hall of Fame. I don’t know if that makes him the greatest golfer of all time, and frankly, I don’t think that matters. I’m just glad I have been able to watch.How good a golfer was Tiger Woods?There’s a really easy way to answer this, as someone who’s about his age and has followed his career since his college days. You never doubted he’d make the putt. That simple, really. Perhaps the single best example is THAT PUTT at the 2008 US Open. I absolutely, positively knew he was going to roll that one in. The surprise would have been if he missed it.As Jim Nantz said - “Expect anything different?” A 12 footer to force a playoff to win the US Open? The incredible pressure to make that would destroy most players. You just don’t see anyone step up and make a putt like that too often. But I knew - as I’m sure he did - he’d make that putt. That’s how good Tiger was. As far as I’m concerned, that’s one of the greatest putts of all time.How good a golfer was Tiger Woods?It's a great question and this debate will rage on for years to come. For me it's quite simple. But there's no doubt in my mind that he is the greatest golfer of all time.What is the opinion of Tiger Woods being one of the greatest golfers ever even though he's no longer playing professionally anymore?First of all, he IS still playing professionally, albeit a very limited schedule due to his physical issues (some of which are self-inflicted, so I’m not suggesting he deserves our pity here). And yes, he’s one of the greatest golfers ever, and perhaps would have gone down in sports history as having the greatest individual golf career even if not for some of these self-inflicted wounds. But we can’t speculate on what might have happened, we can only look at what actually happened - I would say that Jack Nicklaus gets the nod for best golf career of all-time, and Tiger is in the running with Ben Hogan for the #2 position - they played in such different eras that a comparison between the two is quite difficult.Who would you rank as the "best Golfer Ever" ahead of Jack Nicklaus?Ben Hogan. Period. When a reporter asked Lee Trevino who was better, SuperMex said, “Well, I've seen Jack Nicklaus watch Hogan hit balls, but I've never seen Hogan watch Jack.” What Hogan did AFTER the bus crash is simply unmatched, even by Tiger. In 1953 he teed it up 6 times. He won 5, including 3 majors. He came in second in the 6th. He'd probably have won the PGA also but he had to choose between it or the British Open because of scheduling. He's the greatest ball striker and most consistent striker that ever lived. In those days, the caddy stood downrange to pick up the balls. Hogan hit his caddy on the head, knocking him down. Before he got up, he hit him 2 more times. Well into his 80s, he came to his club in Ft. Worth after a very long absence. The pro brought his bag out from the back room and dusted it off. Hogan took his driver and walked out to the 9th tee with 4 balls. The club pro watched from the pro shop. Hogan hit the first ball the sort of shook his head and was obviously agitated with the result. He then hit the remaining 3, returned to the shop and put his driver away and left. The pro walked down the 9th fairway to collect the balls. He found the first about 3 yards from the others. The remaining 3, he said, “You could cover with a blanket.” And they were all in perfect position for the approach shot. One more story… Hogan, in his 70s, was playing a friendly round with some golfers from the University of Texas. One of them was a hot shot, anxious to show up the old legend. On a par 3, the kid shot after Hogan, who was about 6′ away from the hole. His shot stopped at about 5′ and he smiled at Hogan as they walked to the green and said, “You're away Mr. Hogan.” The next par 3, the kid was laying about 5′ away. Hogan struck his shot, casually picked up his tee without even looking at his ball in flight. As the ball was just reaching its pinnacle, he said to the kid, “You're away.” And he was.
